question: Why would you pass a nasogastric (NG) tube for a patient dealing with a bowel obstruction?
explanation: When the bowel is blocked, nothing moves down. An NG tube helps drain out built-up gas and fluid so the patient's stomach feels much relieved! Great job keeping this clinical logic clear. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h1)

question: A patient is unconscious and unable to swallow safely. What is a main reason to insert an NG tube?

options.A: To permanently cure the underlying brain injury
options.B: To provide safe enteral nutrition and hydration
options.C: To prevent the patient from moving in bed
options.D: To replace the need for routine oral hygiene care

explanation: If a patient can't swallow safely, we still need to feed them! An NG tube lets us deliver food and water straight to the stomach without choking risks. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h1)

question: In which of these situations would passing an NG tube through the nose be a huge NO-GO (contraindication)?

options.A: History of controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus
options.B: Localized skin infection on the lower leg
options.C: Mild chronic hypertension managed with medication
options.D: Severe facial trauma with a suspected skull fracture

explanation: Spotting a skull fracture means you never want to push anything through the nose—otherwise, the tube could accidentally find its way into the brain! Safety first. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h2)

question: Your patient starts coughing uncontrollably and gets short of breath during a tube feeding. What's the most likely issue?
explanation: Coughing and breathing trouble during a feed are classic warning signs that the feed or tube has slipped into the airway. Always stop and check right away! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h2)

question: What kind of lubricant should you put on the tip of an NG tube before sliding it in?
explanation: Always use a water-soluble jelly! If a tiny bit accidentally goes into the lungs, the body absorbs it safely without causing nasty lung issues. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h3)

question: Why do we check both of the patient's nostrils before putting in an NG tube?

options.A: To check if the patient's blood pressure is stable
options.B: To determine if the patient has a normal gag reflex
options.C: To select the nostril with better airflow and fewer obstructions
options.D: To measure the exact circumference of the patient's head

explanation: Checking both sides helps you pick the clearer, smoother path, making the procedure much more comfortable for your patient. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h3)

question: When measuring how long an NG tube needs to be, what do the letters NEX stand for?

options.C: Nose to Earlobe to Xiphoid process

explanation: N-E-X stands for Nose to Earlobe to Xiphoid process. It's the classic bedside trick to estimate the exact length needed to reach the stomach. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h4)

question: While you are sliding an NG tube down, the patient suddenly coughs hard and turns a bit blue. What should you do immediately?

options.A: Listen with a stethoscope over the epigastric area
options.B: Immediately withdraw the tube into the pharynx
options.C: Encourage the patient to drink more water quickly
options.D: Push the tube in faster to get past the vocal cords

explanation: Coughing and turning bluish means the tube has wandered into the windpipe instead of the food pipe. Pull it back right away to let them breathe easily again! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is the absolute gold standard method to confirm an NG tube is sitting correctly?

options.B: Auscultating an air bolus over the stomach
options.C: Observing condensation inside the clear plastic tube
options.D: Checking if the patient can speak clearly

explanation: An X-ray never guesses! It gives you a clear picture of exactly where the tube tip is resting, making it the top gold standard. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h5)

question: You test fluid pulled from a newly placed NG tube and find a pH of 4.0. What does this tell you?

options.A: The patient is experiencing severe lung infection.
options.B: The tube is correctly placed in the stomach.
options.C: The tube is coiled inside the patient's esophagus.
options.D: The tube has accidentally entered the lungs.

explanation: Stomach acid is nice and acidic, usually sitting between pH 1.0 and 5.5. A pH of 4.0 is a great sign you are in the right spot! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h5)

question: How often should you flush a continuous feeding NG tube with water to keep it clear?
explanation: Flushing every 4 to 6 hours keeps the formula from drying out and blocking the tube. Regular maintenance keeps things flowing smoothly! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h6)

question: Why is it so important to tape and secure the NG tube firmly to the patient's nose?

options.A: To stop the stomach from producing normal digestive acids
options.B: To prevent friction and trauma to the nasal mucosa from tube movement
options.C: To make the tube completely invisible from the outside
options.D: To ensure the patient can easily remove the tube themselves

explanation: If the tube slides around, it rubs against delicate nose tissue and causes painful sores. Securing it well keeps your patient comfortable. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h6)

question: What size syringe should you use when trying to clear a blocked nasogastric tube?
explanation: Always grab a 30 mL or bigger syringe! Small syringes build up too much pressure and can burst the plastic tubing, whereas bigger syringes spread out the force safely. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h7)

question: A patient with an NG tube suddenly feels nauseous and bloated. What should you check first?

options.A: Administer a strong oral tablet for pain relief
options.B: Check gastric residual volume and assess tube patency
options.C: Increase the speed of the tube feeding pump immediately
options.D: Pull the entire tube out right away without checking

explanation: Nausea and bloating usually mean the food isn't draining or emptying properly. Checking how much fluid is left in the stomach (residuals) and making sure the tube isn't clogged is your best first step. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h7)

question: What instruction should you give your patient right before you pull out an NG tube?

options.A: Breathe in and out through your mouth very fast
options.B: Suck on a hard candy immediately
options.C: Take a deep breath and hold it
options.D: Cough as hard as you can

explanation: Holding a deep breath closes their vocal cords, protecting their airway from any drips as you slide the tube out. Smart nursing technique! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h8)

question: Why do we pull an NG tube out in one quick, smooth motion?

options.A: To minimize patient discomfort and reduce gagging
options.B: To ensure the stomach stays permanently inflated
options.C: To make sure the tape stays attached to the nose
options.D: To prevent the tube from breaking into tiny pieces

explanation: Doing it smoothly and quickly gets it over with fast, saving your patient from extra throat irritation and gagging. You've got this! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T1#GNS212_U1_T1_h8)
